paragraphs.text: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia type III (FHH3) is an autosomal dominant disorder of extracellular calcium homeostasis that affects the parathyroids, kidneys, and bone. Like the other forms of FHH, it causes lifelong high serum calcium with inappropriately low urinary calcium excretion. Nesbit et al. (2013) noted that FHH3 also shows increased serum parathyroid hormone (PTH), hypophosphatemia, and osteomalacia. All reported mutations are heterozygous missense changes at arg15 of the sigma-2 subunit of adaptor protein-2 (AP2), which is encoded by AP2S1 (Nesbit et al., 2013).

paragraphs.text: McMurtry et al. (1992) described a large kindred with familial benign (hypocalciuric) hypercalcemia. After the proposita was identified, 46 family members spanning 5 generations and aged 1.5 to 91 years were surveyed biochemically and/or by chart review, and 19 were found to be affected. In the 15 hypercalcemic subjects studied biochemically, serum immunoreactive PTH, measured in 3 separate immunoassays, became supranormal by about age 30 years and appeared to rise further thereafter. Serum alkaline phosphatase activity and creatinine were normal, but inorganic phosphate was lower than in unaffected family members. Of 5 affected adults older than 40 years who were studied radiographically, 3 had changes suggestive of osteomalacia. In one of them, a 51-year-old woman, iliac crest biopsy after tetracycline labeling confirmed defective skeletal mineralization. McMurtry et al. (1992) concluded that in this kindred the disorder could be especially hard to distinguish from primary hyperparathyroidism in adults, and that it might not be entirely benign, because osteomalacia, perhaps due to mild hypophosphatemia, could develop in adulthood.

paragraphs.text: Fujisawa et al. (2013) reported a Japanese girl whose hypercalcemia was found on routine laboratory testing for poor weight gain on breastfeeding. At 49 days of age her serum calcium, adjusted by Payne's formula, was 13.1 mg/dL, intact PTH was 27 pg/mL, and urinary calcium-to-creatinine ratio was 1.29 mg/mg. There was no evidence of hyperparathyroidism, a PTHrP-producing neoplasm, or vitamin D excess. The authors concluded that absence of hypocalciuria does not necessarily argue against an AP2S1 mutation, and suggested that the patient's early infantile age played a role in her hypercalciuria.

paragraphs.text: Howles et al. (2016) described 3 previously unreported, unrelated probands with FHH3 and symptomatic hypercalcemia. A 34-year-old woman with a 12-year history of hypercalcemia had fatigue, headaches, and persistent generalized aches that did not resolve after parathyroidectomy. A 22-year-old man had hypercalcemia, fatigue, and generalized rib pain. A 52-year-old woman with about a 20-year history of hypercalcemia had headaches, abdominal pain, vomiting, fatigue, and musculoskeletal pain that did not resolve after pamidronate infusion or parathyroidectomy. Howles et al. (2016) described FHH3 as the most clinically severe form of familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia.

paragraphs.text: Nesbit et al. (2013) performed exome sequencing on 1 affected member of each of 2 unrelated FHH3 kindreds, from Oklahoma and from Northern Ireland. Within the 3.46-Mbp FHH3 interval on 19q13.3, they found a single shared variant, a C-to-T transition in exon 2 of the AP2S1 gene that predicted an arg15-to-cys (R15C) substitution. The change was confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Restriction enzyme analysis showed that it cosegregated with disease in 32 affected and 23 unaffected members from 4 generations of the 2 kindreds. The authors then sequenced AP2S1 in 50 unrelated FHH patients without CASR mutations and found 11 heterozygous missense mutations, all affecting arg15: 4 R15C, 3 arg15-to-his (R15H), and 4 arg15-to-leu (R15L). Arg15 is conserved in all AP2-sigma-2 orthologs and in the human AP sigma paralogs, and the crystal structure of AP2 showed that it contacts the dileucine motifs of cargo proteins. In HEK293 cells stably expressing CaSR, all 3 mutants shifted the concentration-response curves to the right, with higher EC50 values, indicating reduced sensitivity to extracellular calcium. The R15C mutant raised the EC50 significantly above that of vector alone, suggesting a possible dominant-negative effect. Wild-type AP2S1 increased calcium-stimulated CaSR internalization, but the R15C mutant did not. In addition, mutating the CaSR C-terminal dileucine motif reduced CaSR signaling.

paragraphs.text: Howles et al. (2016) reported a proband with symptomatic hypercalcemia who carried a heterozygous R15L mutation and responded to cinacalcet.

checks.claim: A proband with symptomatic hypercalcemia carried a heterozygous AP2S1 R15L mutation.
checks.evidence_quote: Each of the three probands had an AP2S1 mutation causing an Arg15Cys, Arg15His, or Arg15Leu substitution (Fig. 1A).
checks.explanation: One of the probands carried the heterozygous Arg15Leu (R15L) mutation.

checks.claim: The proband with symptomatic hypercalcemia and a heterozygous AP2S1 R15L mutation responded to cinacalcet.
checks.evidence_quote: cinacalcet can reduce the symptoms of familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia type 3 associated with all three AP2S1 mutations.
checks.explanation: The paper says all three probands, including the R15L carrier, responded to cinacalcet.
